evidence: Liv. 21.58.3: adeō atrōx adorta tempestās est
terms.comment: Also of storms that fall upon someone.

evidence: Caes. BG 1.12.3: eōs impedītōs et inopīnantēs adgressus
terms.comment: Properly “go up to”; also of approaching a person or tackling a task (see approach).

evidence: Sen. Ep. 104.6: in pāscuum ēmissus cibum meum invāsī
Traupman 188: oppidum oppugnāre, to storm a town

terms.comment: To make an attack on: impetum facere in with the accusative. An attack of illness is also impetus (Traupman 62, 274).

evidence: Caes. BG 4.16: quī sibi Galliaeque bellum intulissent (Lewis & Short s.v. bellum)

terms.latin: vim facere (+ dat. or in + acc.)
evidence: Cic. Caecin. 63: inermibus vim facere (Lewis & Short s.v. inermis)

phrases.latin: Eōs impedītōs et inopīnantēs adgressus magnam partem eōrum concīdit
phrases.english: He attacked them while they were encumbered and off their guard, and cut down a great part of them

phrases.latin: adeō atrōx adorta tempestās est, ut Alpium prope foeditātem superāverit
phrases.english: so fierce a storm fell on them that it almost outdid the horrors of the Alps

phrases.latin: sē impetum hostium, quantum corpore ūnō posset obsistī, exceptūrum
phrases.english: he would take the enemy’s attack himself, as far as one body could hold it back
to invade (literally “to go in with an army”)
to accuse someone of assault (of violence)
